analysis.one_liner: Makes it much harder for large companies to merge by tightening antitrust rules.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Klobuchar with 5 Democratic cosponsors, never left the Senate Judiciary Committee and never got a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the nation's main merger law, the Clayton Act, to make it easier to block corporate mergers. It would lower the bar for proving a merger is illegal, make big merging companies prove their deal won't hurt competition, create a new FTC office focused on competition, and require companies that settle with antitrust enforcers to report for five years on whether their promised benefits materialized.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, workers, and small businesses. The bill's findings cite consolidation that depresses wages and squeezes suppliers, and it targets exactly those harms: it would make it easier to challenge mergers that create a single dominant buyer (monopsony) — the situation where one big employer or buyer can force low wages and low supplier prices. Small businesses competing against dominant firms would face fewer acquisitions of their rivals by giants.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the current 'substantially lessens competition' standard with 'materially lessens competition,' defined as any harm to competition more than trivial, making it easier for enforcers and state attorneys general to win merger challenges.
Adds 'monopsony' to the Clayton Act, so mergers that create a single dominant buyer — which the bill says can force workers to accept unreasonably low wages — can be blocked.

Shifts the burden of proof: for very large deals (over $5 billion, or deals involving companies worth over $100 billion buying firms worth over $50 million), the merging companies themselves must prove the deal won't materially harm competition.

Creates an Office of the Competition Advocate at the FTC to collect and publish data on market concentration, hear complaints from consumers, small businesses, and workers, and evaluate whether past merger settlements actually worked.

Requires companies that settle merger cases with the FTC or Justice Department to report annually for five years on prices, quality, and whether claimed efficiencies and consumer benefits actually happened.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations that want to acquire other companies. Mergers worth $5 billion or more would face a legal presumption against them, requiring the companies to litigate and prove the deal is harmless. Big companies would also face new reporting duties and data demands from the FTC.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large corporations pursuing mergers and acquisitions

drawbacks.text: The lower 'materially lessens competition' standard could block or raise the cost of mergers that are actually harmless or efficiency-enhancing, since companies would bear the legal burden of proving deals over $5 billion are benign even when consumers benefit from them.
Companies would face five years of mandatory reporting on pricing, quality, and claimed efficiencies after settling a merger case, adding compliance costs on top of the settlement itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a deliberate rebalancing: current courts place a heavy proof burden on the government, and the bill flips that burden onto large acquirers. The main cost is that some mergers that would have helped consumers may be deterred or delayed by the new legal hurdle, and large firms bear added compliance costs. Supporters argue decades of rising concentration — the bill cites over $10 trillion in mergers since 2008 — show the current standard fails workers and consumers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Klobuchar introduced the bill on January 31, 2019, joined by original cosponsors including Sen. Markey, Sen. Blumenthal, and Sen. Booker.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary — the only action the bill ever received.
The bill attracted 5 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no further action before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large companies and industries that benefit from mergers and acquisitions are better off, because the merger law was never changed and the courts' pro-merger reading stayed in place.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, and Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill after referral; it received no hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats (the sponsor plus 5 Democratic cosponsors), and no Republican support is recorded; the bill died in committee without any vote.

industries.industry: Large corporate acquirers and private equity
industries.note: The bill would presume harm for mergers above $5 billion and force those companies to prove deals don't reduce competition, raising the cost and risk of the roughly $10 trillion in M&A activity the bill cites since 2008. Blocking anticompetitive deals is precisely the benefit to consumers, workers, and small suppliers.

The bill targets monopsony power, where one dominant buyer forces suppliers and workers to accept lower prices and wages, and would make it harder for large firms to acquire small competitors. Small firms would face fewer dominant buyers and acquirers dictating terms.

industries.industry: Antitrust defense bar and merger consultants
industries.note: With the burden of proof shifted to merging companies for large deals, companies would need more legal and economic defense work for contested mergers — but the bill would also reduce the volume of large mergers overall, cutting the business these firms advise on.
